messages.subject: R 3.0.2 upgrade
messages.body_plain:
I've started on merging the R 3.0.2 changes into the CXXR codebase.  A couple of questions:

Are there any parts other than src/main/ where the merge requires significant manual work?

I've seen four different cast styles in CXXR:
      static_cast<int>(foo)
      (int) foo
      int(foo)
      CXXRCONSTRUCT(int, foo)

I think the last of these is used where CR doesn't have a cast at all, so that uncxxr can do it's magic.
There are a number of cases where CR has '(int) foo' and CXXR has 'int(foo)', which leads to extra conflicts while merging code.  Is there a particular reason for this change?

I'm sure I'll have more questions as I go...

Thanks,

Karl

messages.subject: Re: R 3.0.2 upgrade
messages.body_plain:
On Friday, 18 October 2013 04:10:47 UTC+1, Karl Millar  wrote:
...

> I've seen four different cast styles in CXXR:
>       static_cast<int>(foo)
>       (int) foo
>       int(foo)
>       CXXRCONSTRUCT(int, foo)
>
> I think the last of these is used where CR doesn't have a cast at all, so that uncxxr can do it's magic.
> There are a number of cases where CR has '(int) foo' and CXXR has 'int(foo)', which leads to extra conflicts while merging code.  Is there a particular reason for this change?

Well, you're right about CXXRCONSTRUCT.

(int)foo is a C-style cast.  I hate these: what they do can range from the innocuous to the villainous, and they're difficult to locate using e.g. grep.  So when I upgrade CXXR to a new release of CR, I try compiling everything with '-Wold-style-cast -Werror', and replace any C-style casts with an alternative, in this case a C++ constructor expression int(foo).  uncxxr.pl <http://uncxxr.pl> will do its best to reverse this change, so that substantive changes in the CR code can more easily be found.

I generally use static_cast<T>(foo) only when the target typename T isn't a single token; otherwise the constructor form is more concise (and, I believe, enforces the same level of type safety).

Unfortunately some system header files (on Linux) contain C-style casts, so -Wold-style-cast sometimes shows false positives.

Andrew
